# Ten Years of Morning Runs — What I Found When I Let Go

Ten years.

From the spring I turned thirty-two, I woke at 5:30 every morning and ran five kilometres. Through rain. Around hotels on business trips. It wasn't just a habit. It was **part of who I was**.

And then, last winter, I stopped.

## What My Knee Taught Me

It started with pain in my right knee. The orthopaedist's verdict: a thinning meniscus. His advice? "Three times a week at most."

Honestly, three times a week would have been enough. But I stopped entirely.

Here's the thing: running every morning had become a rule. Skipping a single morning felt like it would shatter the whole rule — and with it, something deeper.

## A New Ritual: Evening Walks

Instead, I began walking the dog for forty minutes each evening.

At first, it felt like something was missing:

- No breathlessness
- No sweat
- No sense of achievement

But around the second week, something shifted. My mind was quieter on those walks.

The key takeaway is that while running, I had only ever thought about pace and distance.

## What I Truly Loved

It wasn't running I loved. It was **time when I didn't have to talk to anyone**.

Perhaps this is the profound truth that ten years led me to. The morning half hour used to be that time. Now, the evening forty minutes play that role.

## Looking Ahead

My knee still aches a little. In spring, I might try running again — twice a week, starting with short distances.

But not as a rule. Only on the mornings I want to.

Letting go isn't about losing something. It's about opening the door to new possibilities.
